name: Sumbawa
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Shiohara, Asako 2006, A Grammar of Sumbawa (in Japanese), PhD diss., University of Tokyo; not online. Wikipedia phonology section (read) has no stress statement.

new_statements.quote: In Sumbawa, the stress is located on the final syllable of each word (e.g., kawa ‘coffee’, nginom ‘drink’, in which stressed syllables are underlined) 4. A subject prefix and an AM clitic are always pronounced without stress. The former is attached to the predicate head (e.g., ku-laló ‘I go’, sia-kakan ‘you eat’), while the latter may phonologically attach to the subsequent constituent, if any, to form a stress unit. [fn.4:] Some words are lexically stressed more strongly than other words, and in some cases, the existence or absence of such stress may cause a distinction in meaning. Such stronger lexical stress is indicated by an apostrophe, as in the following examples: tunóng’ ‘sleep’ tunóng ‘burn’; popo’ ‘make a magic’ popo ‘wash’
new_statements.citation: Shiohara, Asako. 2013. Tense, aspect, mood and polarity in the Sumbawa Besar dialect of Sumbawa. In John Bowden (ed.), Tense, aspect, mood and evidentiality in languages of Indonesia. NUSA 55: 173-192. [hdl:10108/74332]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word (stressed syllable longer and louder per NUSA 56 p.142). Pronominal subject proclitics/genitive enclitics, aspect-mood clitics, future ya, and (normally) past ka and invitational ma are unstressed and join an adjacent word in one stress unit whose single stress is on the unit's last syllable; negators nó, siong and prohibitive na are always stressed. No weight or vowel-quality conditions are stated.
new_statements.exceptions: A lexical class of words carries 'stronger than usual' final stress, occasionally meaning-distinguishing (tunóng' vs tunóng, popo' vs popo), written with a word-final apostrophe; Shiohara 2009 (AALL 4, pp.78-79) adds that on words ending in an open syllable or -ng this may surface as a glottal stop or falling pitch depending on syntactic position, and Shiohara 2025 (AALL 19) rewrites these words with a final phonemic glottal stop /ʔ/. Clitics are stressless; in purposive serial verbs and undergoer incorporation the first element loses its stress and the whole unit carries one final stress (AALL 1 p.47; NUSA 54 sec.3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word, extended to a 'stress unit' (word plus clitics/demonstratives, incorporated V+N, SVC V1+V2) whose single stress falls on the unit-final syllable; statements are based on conversational field data from the Sumbawa Besar dialect, impressionistic (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: All of Shiohara's statements describe the Sumbawa Besar dialect (data from Sumbawa Besar town and Empang, central Sumbawa), which she says serves as the inter-dialect lingua franca; the other dialects (Taliwang, Jereweh, Tongo) are not covered. Glottolog language-level code sumb1241 applies; dialect-level code not verified.

sources.note: p.175: stress is located on the final syllable of each word (kawa, nginom); subject prefixes and AM clitics always unstressed; clitics form stress units with hosts; fn.4: some words carry lexically stronger stress, sometimes meaning-distinguishing, marked with apostrophe (tunóng' 'sleep' vs tunóng 'burn', popo' vs popo); pp.176: ka, ma normally unstressed, negators nó/siong and na always stressed.

sources.note: p.142: 'word-level stress is located on the final syllable of each word... A stressed syllable is pronounced longer and louder than other syllables. The clitics ku, mu, tu are, however, pronounced without stress'; demonstratives/genitive clitics fall within the stress domain of the preceding noun.

sources.note: fn.1: apostrophe marks word-final stress heavier than usual (sólé'); sec.3.2: 'In Sumbawa, word stress normally occurs on the last syllable of each word'; under undergoer incorporation verb+noun carry one stress on the noun's final syllable.

sources.note: appendix pp.78-79: 'この言語では，語の最後に強勢が置かれ，強く発音される' (stress is placed at the end of the word); in some words it is especially strong and, when the word ends in an open syllable or ng, may be accompanied by a glottal stop or falling pitch depending on syntax; such words marked with apostrophe (tunóng'/tunóng, popo'/popo -- glosses reversed relative to NUSA 55).

sources.citation: 塩原朝子 [Shiohara Asako]. 2006. スンバワ語の「移動とその目的」を表す動詞連続構文 ['Purposive' serial verb construction with a directional verb in Sumbawa]. アジア・アフリカの言語と言語学 (Asian and African Languages and Linguistics) 1. hdl:10108/51083
sources.note: sec.2.2 p.47: 'この言語では，単語は通常は最終音節の母音に強勢を伴って発話される' (words are normally uttered with stress on the final-syllable vowel; laló, buya stressed on ó, a); V1 of purposive SVC loses its stress; appendix: some words have especially strong word-final stress, marked with apostrophe (mèsa-mèsa').
